---
title: "3. Challenge: deploying a Hugo website to GitHub Pages"
order: 3
---

In this tutorial you'll put together what you learned in Parts
[1](tutorial1.qmd) and [2](tutorial2.qmd). You'll create a new repository with
a (very) simple website built with [Hugo](https://gohugo.io), then write a
GitHub Actions workflow *on your own* that publishes the website to GitHub
Pages every time you push a change.

Hugo is a *static site generator*: it takes content that you write in
Markdown files, combines it with *templates* that describe how the pages
should look, and produces a website made up of plain HTML files. It's a
popular tool for building personal websites, blogs, and project pages. (This
course website is built with a different static site generator called
[Quarto](https://quarto.org), but the idea is the same.)

## I. Create the website

### 1. Create a repository on GitHub

1.  Go to https://github.com/new to create a new repository.

2.  Under "Owner," select yourself. Under "Repository name," type
    `my-hugo-site`.

3.  Make sure "Public" is selected, and turn on "Add README."

4.  Click the green `Create repository` button.

5.  Clone the repository to your computer, and `cd` into it. (See
    [Part 2](../02_git/cli/exercise2.qmd#ii.-clone-the-repository-to-your-local-computer)
    of the git tutorials if you need a refresher.)

### 2. Install Hugo

The easiest way to install Hugo on any operating system is with conda. Create
a new environment for it:

```bash
conda create -n hugo -c conda-forge hugo
conda activate hugo
```

Check that it worked by running:

```bash
hugo version
```

You should see something like `hugo v0.169.0...`.

### 3. Create the site

1.  From the top level of your `my-hugo-site` repository, run:

    ```bash
    hugo new site . --force
    ```

    This tells Hugo to create a new site in the current directory (`.`).
    Normally Hugo will refuse to create a site in a directory that already has
    files in it; the `--force` tells it to do it anyway (we already have a
    `README.md` here).

2.  Run `ls`. You'll see that Hugo created a bunch of directories, along with a
    file called `hugo.toml`. We only need to worry about a few of them:

    * `hugo.toml`: Hugo's configuration file for the site.
    * `content`: This is where the content of the website goes, written in
      Markdown.
    * `layouts`: This is where the templates go that tell Hugo how to turn
      the content into HTML.

    Most Hugo sites use a *theme* that provides the layouts for you. We'll
    write our own (very simple) layout instead, so that you can see how
    the pieces fit together.

3.  Open `hugo.toml` in your favorite text editor. It will look like:

    ```toml
    baseURL = 'https://example.org/'
    locale = 'en-us'
    title = 'My New Hugo Project'
    ```

    Change the `title` to something you like (e.g., `'My Website'`), and add the
    following line to the end of the file:

    ```toml
    disableKinds = ['taxonomy', 'term']
    ```

    By default, Hugo creates extra pages for organizing blog posts by tags and
    categories (which it calls "taxonomies"). We don't need those for a
    single-page site, and adding this line stops Hugo from warning us that we
    don't have layouts for them. Don't worry about the `baseURL` for now;
    we'll come back to it later.

4.  Now create the layout. Use your favorite text editor to create a file
    called `layouts/home.html` with the following in it:

    ```html
    <!DOCTYPE html>
    <html lang="en">
    <head>
      <meta charset="utf-8">
      <title>{{ .Site.Title }}</title>
    </head>
    <body>
      <h1>{{ .Title }}</h1>
      {{ .Content }}
    </body>
    </html>
    ```

    This is an ordinary HTML file, with a few placeholders in `{{ }}`. When
    Hugo builds the site, it will replace `{{ .Site.Title }}` with the title
    you set in `hugo.toml`, `{{ .Title }}` with the title of the page, and
    `{{ .Content }}` with the content of the page, converted from Markdown to
    HTML. The name `home.html` tells Hugo to use this layout for the home page
    of the site.

5.  Finally, create the content for the home page. Create a file called
    `content/_index.md` and put the following in it:

    ```markdown
    ---
    title: "Welcome to my website!"
    ---

    This website was built with [Hugo](https://gohugo.io/).

    Here are some things I like:

    - Open source software
    - GitHub Actions
    - **Coffee**
    ```

    The part between the `---` lines at the top is called *front matter*.
    It's where you put information about the page, like its title. (You may
    have noticed that the `.qmd` files for this course website have front
    matter, too.) Everything after that is ordinary Markdown. Feel free to
    change the text and list to whatever you like!

### 4. Build the site on your computer

1.  From the top level of your repository, run:

    ```bash
    hugo
    ```

    This builds the site. Hugo will print a table summarizing the pages it
    built. It puts the resulting website in a directory called `public`.

2.  Run `ls public`. You'll see an `index.html` file (along with a couple of
    other files Hugo makes by default). Open `public/index.html` in a text
    editor and take a look. You'll see that Hugo took your layout and filled
    in the placeholders, converting the Markdown in `content/_index.md` into
    HTML (e.g., `**Coffee**` became `<strong>Coffee</strong>`).

3.  Now open `public/index.html` in your web browser (by double-clicking on it,
    or using `open` on Mac, `start` on Windows, or `xdg-open` on Linux, as in
    [Part 2](tutorial2.qmd#build-the-documentation-on-your-computer)). You
    should see your website!

::: {.callout-tip}
While you're working on a Hugo site, you can also run:

```bash
hugo server
```

This builds the site and starts a small web server on your computer. Go to
http://localhost:1313/ in your browser to see the site. While the server is
running, Hugo will rebuild the site and refresh your browser every time you
save a change to one of the files. Hit `<Ctrl>+C` in the terminal to stop the
server.
:::

### 5. Commit and push

1.  As with the Sphinx documentation in Part 2, we don't want to commit the
    generated website. Create a file called `.gitignore` at the top level of
    your repository with the following in it:

    ```bash
    public/
    resources/
    .hugo_build.lock
    ```

    (`resources` and `.hugo_build.lock` are other files that Hugo creates while
    building the site.)

2.  Run `git status` to check that `public` is not listed, then commit
    everything and push:

    ```bash
    git add .
    git commit -m "create hugo site"
    git push
    ```

    Since this is your own repository and you're the only one working on it,
    we're just committing directly to `main` here.

    ::: {.callout-note}
    Hugo creates a few empty directories (like `assets` and `static`). `git`
    doesn't track empty directories, so you won't see these on GitHub. That's
    fine; Hugo doesn't need them.
    :::

## II. Deploy the site with GitHub Actions

:::: {.callout-caution appearance="simple" icon="false"}
#### Challenge

Write a GitHub Actions workflow that builds your Hugo site and deploys it to
GitHub Pages every time you push to `main`. When you're done, your website
should be at `https://YOUR_USERNAME.github.io/my-hugo-site/`.

Use the `docs.yml` workflow you wrote in [Part 2](tutorial2.qmd) as a
starting point. Some hints:

-   Don't forget to set your repository's GitHub Pages "Source" to
    `GitHub Actions` (see
    [Part 2, step 6](tutorial2.qmd#turn-on-github-pages)).
-   Since every push to `main` should deploy the site, you don't need the `if`
    condition on the `deploy` job, or the `pull_request` trigger.
-   You'll need to install Hugo on the runner. You *could* install conda on
    the runner and then use it to install Hugo, but it's easier to use an
    action someone has already written. Search the
    [GitHub Marketplace](https://github.com/marketplace?type=actions) for
    "hugo". The `peaceiris/actions-hugo` action is a popular choice.
-   Remember that Hugo puts the website it builds in `public`.
-   Remember the `baseURL` in `hugo.toml`? Hugo uses it to create links
    between pages. Our one-page site will work without changing it, but it's
    good practice to set it correctly. You can override it when you build by
    running `hugo --baseURL URL`. The
    [`actions/configure-pages`](https://github.com/actions/configure-pages)
    action outputs the URL of your GitHub Pages site as `base_url`, which you
    can use in a later step with `${{ steps.STEP_ID.outputs.base_url }}`
    (where `STEP_ID` is the `id` you give the `configure-pages` step).
    *(This one's optional.)*

Once you've written your workflow, commit it and push it to GitHub, then check
the `Actions` tab to see if it worked. If it didn't, click on the failed job
to see what went wrong, fix it, and push again. That's how everyone writes
workflows!

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon="false"}
##### Solution

1.  Turn on GitHub Pages: go to your repository on GitHub, click `Settings`,
    then `Pages`, and under "Build and deployment" set "Source" to
    `GitHub Actions`.

2.  Create a file called `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` with the following in it:

    ```yaml
    name: Deploy website

    on:
      push:
        branches: [main]

    jobs:
      build:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - name: Check out the repository
            uses: actions/checkout@v7

          - name: Install Hugo
            uses: peaceiris/actions-hugo@v3
            with:
              hugo-version: "0.169.0"

          - name: Get the GitHub Pages URL
            id: pages
            uses: actions/configure-pages@v6

          - name: Build the website
            run: hugo --minify --baseURL "${{ steps.pages.outputs.base_url }}/"

          - name: Upload the website
            uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v5
            with:
              path: public

      deploy:
        needs: build
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        permissions:
          pages: write
          id-token: write
        environment:
          name: github-pages
          url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
        steps:
          - name: Deploy to GitHub Pages
            id: deployment
            uses: actions/deploy-pages@v5
    ```

    The differences from Part 2's `docs.yml` are:

    * The workflow only runs on pushes to `main`, so there's no `if` on the
      `deploy` job.
    * Instead of setting up Python and installing Sphinx, we use
      `peaceiris/actions-hugo` to install Hugo. We set `hugo-version` to the
      same version of Hugo that we used on our own computer, so that the
      site is built the same way in both places.
    * We use `actions/configure-pages` to get the URL of our GitHub Pages
      site, then pass it to `hugo` with `--baseURL`. (The `--minify` option
      tells Hugo to remove unnecessary whitespace from the HTML files to make
      them smaller. It's optional.)
    * We upload `public` instead of `docs/_build/html`.

3.  Commit and push:

    ```bash
    git add .github/workflows/deploy.yml
    git commit -m "add workflow to deploy website"
    git push
    ```

4.  Go to the `Actions` tab on GitHub and click on the running workflow. Once
    the `deploy` job finishes, click on the link under it to see your website.
:::
::::

## III. Update the website

### 6. Make a change

Now that your workflow is set up, updating your website is as easy as pushing
a change.

1.  Open `content/_index.md` and change something. For example, add another
    item to your list, or add a new paragraph at the end.

2.  If you like, preview the change on your computer by running `hugo server`
    (or by running `hugo` and opening `public/index.html`).

3.  Commit and push the change:

    ```bash
    git add -u
    git commit -m "update home page"
    git push
    ```

4.  Go to the `Actions` tab on GitHub. You'll see that your workflow started
    running as soon as you pushed. Once it's done, go to
    `https://YOUR_USERNAME.github.io/my-hugo-site/` and refresh the page. You
    should see your change!

    ::: {.callout-note}
    If you don't see the change right away, wait a minute and try again. Your
    web browser may also be showing you an old copy of the page that it saved
    earlier. If so, do a "hard refresh" by holding down `Shift` while clicking
    your browser's refresh button.
    :::

Congratulations! You've written a workflow from scratch that automatically
publishes a website. You never need to build the site yourself again: just
write Markdown, commit, and push, and GitHub will take care of the rest.
